There are many landmarks worth visiting: There are many landmarks worth visiting in Warsaw, including:
The Old City: It is enough to know that: The Old Town: Its place on the UNESCO World Heritage List is enough to show its value. The town was restored and its buildings painted in distinctive colours to repair the damage it suffered in World War II.
The Royal Palace: One of the most promin: The Royal Palace: One of the city’s most prominent landmarks, the palace contains magnificent royal rooms and halls decorated with paintings and precious antiques. You can visit the palace and learn about the history of Poland as you wander through its halls. Don’t miss the palace gardens and fountains, which transport you to a fairy-tale world.
Warsaw Fortress: The fort is one of the: Warsaw Fortress: The fortress is one of the most prominent historical monuments in Warsaw. It bears witness to important historical events, and a visit is a great opportunity to learn about the region’s military architecture. The massive walls, mighty towers and overall design are an impressive record of the architecture of the era. Wander through its courtyards and enjoy the wonderful view of the surrounding greenery.
Palace of Culture and Science: The palac: Palace of Culture and Science: The palace dates back to the 1950s and was a gift from the Soviet Union to Poland. It stands out for its towering height of 231 metres, with 30 floors, and is part of the old city. The palace is therefore the tallest building in Warsaw and one of the tallest on the European continent. Imagine the panoramic view from the top at such a soaring height. Some of its spaces are given over to cultural performances, art exhibitions, conferences, libraries and theatres, so you can think of the palace as a platform for culture and the arts. You can attend one of its cultural events or theatre performances and capture your visit in photos.

Wroclaw is one of Poland's tourist citie: Wroclaw is one of Poland’s tourist cities, and some call it the city of dwarves, as you can see more than 600 bronze dwarf statues in the city’s squares. The statues commemorate the peaceful protests once held against the communist regime, when protesters wore hats resembling those of fairy-tale dwarves. Indeed, it did not stop there: legends arose about dwarves who lived within the walls of the old city, which was destroyed in the war. Legend has it that people built the modern city and forgot the dwarves inside the old city walls, so the dwarves began placing bronze statues in the streets at night to remind people of the city’s true heritage and the need to revive it.
World War II destroyed about 70% of the: World War II destroyed about 70% of the city, which is said to have been Hitler’s favourite city. When you see pictures of the city in ruins during the war, you will be amazed at how remarkably it was rebuilt and restored to its former splendour and beauty. You can get around the city on foot without a car, as most of the landmarks are close together. You can also visit the Monopol Hotel, from whose balcony overlooking the square Hitler gave his famous speech.
Old Main Market and Penitent Bridge: A l: Old Main Market Square and Penitents’ Bridge: A large shopping area where locals and tourists buy many of their needs. If you visit the city in December, you can enjoy the largest Christmas market. You can also see the Penitents’ Bridge, also known as the Witches’ Bridge, which dates back to the fourteenth century. In the past, those accused of witchcraft were made to walk across it without railings. Those who made it across were deemed witches and executed immediately, while those who slipped or fell were acquitted. The bridge connects the two towers of the Church of St Mary Magdalene and is linked to many myths and stories.
Zoo: The first zoo of its kind in Poland: Zoo: The first zoo of its kind in Poland, home to a huge number of animals. The zoo also includes an exhibition of aquatic creatures that live in the waters of Africa.

Like many mountain destinations, Zakopane lets you hike and enjoy nature in summer and go snowboarding in winter.
There are many destinations in Zakopane: There are many places in Zakopane that are worth visiting, including:
Tatra Park: The park combines the peaks: Tatra Park: The park brings together the peaks of the Tatra Mountains and green valleys in a view like a painting. You can stroll around and walk the trails. Kropoki Street: The vibrant heart of the: Krupówki Street: The vibrant heart of the town, with shops displaying local handicrafts and souvenirs.
Kasprowy Wierch Mountain: You can reach: Kasprowy Wierch: You can reach the summit by cable car and enjoy a view straight out of fairy tales and legends.

Gdańsk is a coastal city with a very spe: Gdańsk is a coastal city with a very special flavour and is considered the amber capital of the world. It is one of Poland’s tourist cities, and at night it has the atmosphere of a scary film: fog fills the streets and the music of a street performer drifts through its alleys, in a scene remarkably like something from the cinema.
There are many places worth visiting in: There are many places worth visiting in Gdańsk, including:
Gdańsk Wooden Crane: It is the largest w: Gdańsk Wooden Crane: The largest wooden crane in Europe, dating back to the Middle Ages. It was used to load ships’ cargo and to repair the masts of large ships.
Mariska Street: The street has the large: Mariacka Street: The street has the largest concentration of amber, which is used in making jewellery and ornaments. Baltic amber is fossilised tree resin washed up along the coast. Most shops offer jewellery made from amber, and you can obtain a certificate confirming that the piece you bought is genuine amber and listing its specifications.
Mariska Church: Mariska or Mary Church h: St Mary’s Church: St Mary’s (Mariacka) Church is of very great artistic and historical value, as it is the largest brick-built Gothic church in the world. The church was completed in 1500 and can hold 25,000 worshippers. The tallest of its towers can be reached by climbing 400 steps, and from the top there is a majestic view of the city. The church is known for its colourful stained-glass windows, wooden altar, royal tomb and astronomical clock. The astronomical clock is very complex and is considered the oldest of its kind in Europe. The church’s interior dates back entirely to the Middle Ages.
St Bridget's Church: The 14th-century ch: St Bridget’s Church: The 14th-century church features the world’s largest amber altar, which is only natural for the amber capital of the world. The church is also famous for its Tomb of Skulls, which holds the skulls of war victims, lined up along a wall in a solemn scene that you can visit.
World War II Museum: You cannot miss vis: World War II Museum: This museum is not to be missed. It tells the story of the war in an organised, chronological way and includes original items dating from the war. As the war began when the Nazis attacked Gdańsk, the museum feels like a biography of the war, one that not only recounts events but also shows the impact of the war on Poland and the whole world. The museum holds more than 2,000 artefacts.
Amber Museum: An ancient 3-storey buildi: Amber Museum: An old 3-storey building dating back to the 16th century. The museum houses a rare collection of amber. Amber is a warm golden colour and sometimes light green. The museum contains wonderful and rare pieces of amber, and you can buy items and accessories made from amber from the stalls selling products in the museum.
